deckInfo.title: Universal Spanish-English Deck
deckInfo.description: Universal Spanish vocabulary list with regionalisms separated into their own category.

cards.logic: Physical conditions like cold, hunger, or fear are internal states you 'have' (Tener), not permanent identity (Ser) or location (Estar).

cards.spanish: Tienes razón. (PR: Tienes la razón, mano)
cards.literalTrap: Tú estás correcto / Tú eres derecho
cards.logic: 'Right' in the sense of correctness means possessing reason ('Tener razón'). 'Derecho' means straight or right-handed.
Native speakers naturally describe appetite as 'having hunger' rather than being an adjective.
Sleepiness is expressed as 'having sleep' (Tengo sueño).
WARNING: 'Estoy caliente' carries explicit sexual connotation in Spanish! To say you are hot due to temperature, always use 'Tengo calor'.
Fear is expressed as possessing fear ('Tener miedo').

cards.literalTrap: Estoy en un apuro / Estoy apurado
cards.logic: Hurry is a state you hold: 'Tengo prisa'.
Guilt or blame is expressed as 'holding the blame' (Tener la culpa).
Age is measured by accumulated years possessed. In Puerto Rico, subject pronouns stay upfront: '¿Cuántos años TÚ tienes?'

cards.spanish: Se me acabó el café, wao.
cards.literalTrap: Yo corrí fuera de café / Me quedé sin café
cards.logic: Accidental events use 'Se + Indirect Object + Verb'. The coffee finished itself ON me ('Se me acabó').
To avoid personal blame for slips, Spanish says 'The keys fell themselves to me'.
Caribbean Spanish prefers the unintentional reflexive 'Se me olvidó los chavos'. (PR slang: 'los chavos').
'The wallet lost itself from me'. Avoids implying you intentionally threw it away.
Unless you intentionally smashed it on the floor, use 'Se me rompió' (It broke on me).
The rice burned itself on me ('Se me quemó el arroz').

cards.spanish: Se me quedó el celular en la casa.
cards.english: I left my phone at home by mistake.
cards.literalTrap: Yo dejé mi teléfono en la casa
cards.logic: Accidental leaving of items uses 'Se me quedó' (It stayed behind on me).

cards.spanish: Él se parece a su papá.
cards.logic: 'Mirar' is visual scanning. 'Parecerse a' means to resemble someone structurally.

cards.literalTrap: Yo extraño tú / Yo pierdo te
cards.logic: 'Hacer falta' literally means 'You cause a missing piece in me'. In PR, 'mi pana' adds warm friendship.
Body parts take the indirect object pronoun: 'Feet cause pain to me' (Me duelen los pies).
'Caber' is spatial fitting (e.g. fitting in a box). Clothes fitting a person use 'Quedar'.

cards.english: I like traditional Puerto Rican food.
cards.literalTrap: Yo me gusto la comida criolla
cards.logic: The food pleases me ('La comida me gusta a mí'). In PR, local traditional food is 'comida criolla'.

cards.spanish: Me importa un bledo. (PR: Me importa un carajo)
cards.logic: 'Importar' works backwards: 'It matters zero to me'.
Caribbean/PR Spanish syntax keeps the subject pronoun BEFORE the verb in questions ('¿Qué tú dices?').
PR cadence uses '¿Para dónde TÚ vas?' rather than literal '-ing' progressive forms.

cards.english: What do you want to eat?
cards.logic: Iconic Puerto Rican pre-verbal subject placement ('¿Qué tú quieres...?').
'How do you call yourself?' with PR pronoun position: '¿Cómo TÚ te llamas?'
Object pronouns attach BEFORE conjugated verbs: Indirect Object (Te) + Direct Object (lo) + Verb (dije).
Command forms attach object pronouns directly to the end: Dá + me + lo.
Negative commands push pronouns back in FRONT of the verb: 'No me lo des'.

cards.spanish: No creo que vaya a llover hoy, viste.
cards.english: I don't think it's gonna rain today.
cards.literalTrap: No pienso es va a llover hoy
cards.logic: Negated belief ('No creo') triggers subjunctive ('vaya'). 'Viste' is a standard PR check tag.

cards.spanish: No pienso que él tenga razón.
cards.logic: Negating 'Pienso' creates doubt, demanding subjunctive ('tenga') instead of indicative ('tiene').

cards.spanish: Dudo que vengan a la fiesta.
cards.english: I doubt they'll come to the party.
cards.literalTrap: Yo dudo ellos van a venir
cards.logic: 'Dudar' expresses doubt, requiring subjunctive 'vengan'.

cards.spanish: Es importante que tú lo hagas, pa.
cards.english: It's important that you do it.
cards.logic: Impersonal clause + specific subject triggers subjunctive ('hagas').

cards.spanish: Antes de que te vayas, dime.
cards.logic: 'Antes de que' always triggers subjunctive ('vayas').

cards.english: I hope the weather is good.
cards.literalTrap: Yo espero el tiempo es bueno
cards.logic: 'Ojalá' (Arabic origin 'God willing') strictly requires subjunctive 'haga'.

cards.notes: Essential transition word to connect ideas smoothly without pausing.
Extremely common native filler when clarifying what you just said.
Used at the beginning of a sentence to pause or transition thoughts.

cards.english: the thing is... / it's just that
cards.notes: Native way to introduce an explanation or polite excuse.
Used to introduce a new related topic gracefully.
Replaces literal translation trap 'actualmente' (which means currently!).
Used to reinforce or expand on a point you made.
Casual phrase spoken while thinking of an answer.
Expresses relief about a situation ('menos mal que viniste').
Used to summarize or bring a conversation topic to a close.
Common phrase for precautions ('Lleva un paraguas por si acaso').
More formal way of saying 'pero' (but).
Adds extra information to your sentence smoothly.
Used when finding a positive aspect ('al menos hace buen tiempo').
Great narrative opener when telling a story or sharing news.
Common uncertainty phrase along with 'quizás'.
Explains cause ('ya que estás aquí, hablemos').

cards.english: at the end of the day / after all
cards.notes: Used for concluding statements.
Logical connector for cause and effect.

cards.spanish: por un lado... por otro lado
cards.english: on one hand... on the other hand
cards.notes: Used to balance two contrasting points.
Used for alternatives ('en vez de café, quiero té').
Can mean doing something intentionally or changing topics.

cards.english: that is to say / in other words
cards.notes: Formal equivalent of 'o sea'.
Used when stating the final point in a list.
Used to return to a main topic despite interruptions.
